title: The place above the heavens was sung before Plato
source_text: Ἑξῆς δὲ τούτοις φησὶν ὁ Κέλσος παρακούσαντάς τινας Χριστιανοὺς Πλατωνικῶν λέξεων αὐχεῖν τὸν ὑπερουράνιον θεὸν, ὑπεραναβαίνοντας τὸν Ἰουδαίων οὐρανόν. ἐν τούτοις δὲ οὐ διασαφεῖ, πότερον καὶ τὸν Ἰουδαίων θεὸν ὑπεραναβαίνουσιν ἢ μόνον ὃν ὀμνύουσιν οὐρανόν. περὶ μὲν οὖν τῶν ἕτερον ἐπαγγελλομένων θεὸν παρὰ τὸν καὶ ὑπὸ Ἰουδαίων προσκυνούμενον οὐ πρόκειται νῦν ἡμῖν λέγειν, περὶ δὲ ἑαυτῶν ἀπολογεῖσθαι καὶ δεικνύναι ὅτι οὐ δύνανται οἱ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν Ἰουδαίων προφῆται ἀπὸ Πλάτωνός τι εἰληφέναι· πρεσβύτεροι γὰρ ἦσαν αὐτοῦ. οὔτ᾿ οὖν τὴν φάσκουσαν λέξιν· „περὶ τὸν πάντων βασιλέα πάντ᾿ ἐστὶ. καὶ ἐκείνου ἕνεκα πάντα“ ἀπὸ Πλάτωνος εἰλήφαμεν, ἀλλὰ τούτων κρειττόνως εἰρημένα ἀπὸ τῶν προφητῶν μεμαθήκαμεν, σαφηνίσαντος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ τῶν μαθητῶν αὐτοῦ τὸ βούλημα τοῦ ἐν τοῖς προφήταις πνεύματος (ὅπερ οὐκ ἄλλο ἦν τοῦ πνεύματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ), οὔτε τὰ περὶ τοῦ ὑπερουρανίου τόπου πρῶτος ὁ φιλόσοφος παρίστησιν, ἀλλὰ Δαυῒδ τὴν βαθύτητα τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ἐν τοῖς ὑπεραναβεβηκόσι τὰ αἰσθητὰ τῶν περὶ θεοῦ θεωρημάτων πάλαι παρέστησεν εἰπὼν ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῶν ψαλμῶν· „αἰνεῖτε τὸν θεὸν οἱ οὐρανοὶ τῶν οὐρανῶν, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ τὸ ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν· αἰνεσάτωσαν τὸ ὄνομα κυρίου.“ ἐγὼ δὲ οὐκ ἀπογινώσκω τὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ Φαίδρου λέξεις ἀπό τινων Ἑβραίων μεμαθηκότα τὸν Πλάτωνα, ὡς δέ τινες ἀνέγραψαν, ἔτι καὶ τοῖς προφητικοῖς ἐντυχόντα λόγοις ἐκτεθεῖσθαι, ἐν οἷς ἔλεγεν· „τὸν ὑπερουράνιον τόπον οὔτε τις ὕμνησε τῶν τῇδε ποιητὴς οὔτε ὑμνήσει κατ᾿ ἀξίαν“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, ἐν οἷς ἐστι καὶ τὸ„ἡ γὰρ ἀχρώματός τε καὶ ἀσχημάτιστος καὶ ἀναφὴς οὐσία ὄντως οὖσα ψυχῆς κυβερνήτῃ νῷ μόνῳ θεατὴ, περὶ ὅν τὸ τῆς ἀληθοῦς ἐπιστήμης γένος τοῦτον ἔχει τὸν τόπον.“ καὶ ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων γε τῶν λόγων παιδευθεὶς ὁ Παῦλος ἡμῶν καὶ ποθῶν τὰ ὑπερκόσμια καὶ ὑπερου ράνια καὶ δι᾿ ἐκεῖνα πάντα πράττων, ἵν᾿ αὐτῶν τύχῃ, φησὶν ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ πρὸς Κορινθίους ἐπιστολῇ· „τὸ γὰρ παραυτίκα ἐλαφρὸν τῆς θλίψεως ἡμῶν καθ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολὴν αἰώνιον βάρος δόξης κατεργάζεται ἡμῖν. μὴ σκοπούντων ἡμῶν τὰ βλεπόμενα ἀλλὰ τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα· τὰ γὰρ βλεπόμενα πρόσκαιρα, τὰ δὲ μὴ βλεπόμενα αἰώνια.“
pass_a_gloss: Next after these Celsus says that some Christians, having misheard (παρακούω) Platonic sayings, boast (αὐχέω) of the supercelestial God (ὑπερουράνιος θεός), going up beyond (ὑπεραναβαίνω) the heaven (οὐρανός) of the Jews. In these he does not make clear (διασαφέω) whether they go up beyond also the God of the Jews or only the heaven by which they swear (ὀμνύω). About those proclaiming (ἐπαγγέλλομαι) another God besides the one worshipped (προσκυνέω) also by Jews it does not lie before us (πρόκειται) now to speak, but about ourselves to defend (ἀπολογέομαι) and to show that the prophets of the Jews among us cannot have taken (λαμβάνω) anything from Plato; for they were older (πρεσβύτεροι) than him. Neither then the saying stating 'About the king of all are all things, and for his sake all things' did we take from Plato, but things said better (κρειττόνως) than these we have learned from the prophets, Jesus and his disciples having made clear (σαφηνίζω) the intent (βούλημα) of the Spirit (πνεῦμα) in the prophets (which was no other than the Spirit of Christ); nor does the philosopher first present the things about the supercelestial place (ὑπερουράνιος τόπος), but David long ago (πάλαι) presented the depth (βαθύτης) of the multitude (πλῆθος) of the contemplations (θεωρήματα) about God in the things having gone beyond (ὑπεραναβαίνω, pf. ptc.) sensible things (τὰ αἰσθητά), saying in the book of Psalms: 'Praise (αἰνέω) God, the heavens of the heavens, and the water above (ὑπεράνω) the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord (κύριος).' I do not despair of / reject (ἀπογινώσκω) Plato having learned the sayings from the Phaedrus from some Hebrews, and, as some have recorded (ἀναγράφω), also having met with (ἐντυγχάνω) the prophetic words (προφητικοὶ λόγοι), to have set them out, in which he said: 'The supercelestial place neither did any of the poets here (τῇδε) hymn (ὑμνέω) nor will hymn worthily' and what follows, in which is also: 'For the colourless (ἀχρώματος) and shapeless (ἀσχημάτιστος) and intangible (ἀναφής) being (οὐσία) truly being, visible (θεατή) only to mind, pilot (κυβερνήτης) of soul, about which the kind (γένος) of true knowledge (ἐπιστήμη) has this place.' And instructed (παιδεύω) from those words our Paul, and longing for (ποθέω) the things beyond the world (ὑπερκόσμια) and beyond heaven (ὑπερουράνια) and for them doing all things, that he may attain (τυγχάνω) them, says in the second Letter to the Corinthians: 'For the momentary (παραυτίκα) lightness (ἐλαφρόν) of our affliction (θλῖψις) works out (κατεργάζομαι) for us beyond measure to beyond measure (καθ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν) an eternal (αἰώνιον) weight (βάρος) of glory (δόξα), we not looking at (σκοπέω) the things seen but the things not seen; for the things seen are temporary (πρόσκαιρα), but the things not seen eternal.'
pass_b_english: Next after this Celsus says that some Christians, having misunderstood the words of Plato, boast of “the God above the heavens,” climbing up past “the heaven of the Jews.” Here he does not make clear whether they climb past the God of the Jews as well, or only past the heaven by which the Jews swear. It is not our task now to speak about those who proclaim another God besides the one whom the Jews also worship; our task is to defend ourselves and to show that the prophets of the Jews whom we accept cannot have taken anything from Plato, for they were older than he.

So we did not take from Plato the saying “All things are about the King of all, and all things are for his sake.” We have learned from the prophets things said better than these, since Jesus and his disciples made plain the meaning of the Spirit who was in the prophets, who was none other than the Spirit of Christ (1 Peter 1:11). Nor is the philosopher the first to set forth what concerns the place above the heavens. Long ago David set forth the depth of the many insights about God that belong to the realms beyond the things of sense, when he said in the book of Psalms: “Praise God, you heavens of heavens, and the water that is above the heavens; let them praise the name of the Lord” (Psalm 148:4–5).

For my part, I do not rule out that Plato learned the words in the Phaedrus from certain Hebrews and, as some have recorded, had even come upon the prophetic writings when he set them out. There he said: “The place above the heavens no poet here below has ever yet sung, nor ever will sing, as it deserves,” and what follows (Plato, Phaedrus 247c), among which is this too: “For the being that truly is, colourless, shapeless and intangible, visible only to mind, the pilot of the soul, the being with which the true kind of knowledge is concerned, holds this place” (Plato, Phaedrus 247c).

And our Paul, trained by those very prophetic words, longing for what lies beyond the world and beyond the heavens and doing everything for its sake, that he might attain it, says in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: “For our momentary light affliction is working out for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory, as we look not at what is seen but at what is not seen; for what is seen is temporary, but what is not seen is eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:17–18).

choices.choice: Celsus’s charge is reported in indirect speech; only his two key phrases (τὸν ὑπερουράνιον θεόν, τὸν Ἰουδαίων οὐρανόν) are put in quotation marks. ‘The heaven by which they swear’ alludes to Celsus’s earlier claim (see 5.6) that the Jews worship heaven; compare Matthew 5:34 on swearing by heaven; not cited inline because Origen is reporting Jewish practice, not quoting Scripture. ‘Another God’ = the Marcionite and gnostic claim of a higher God than the Creator; capitalised because they mean it of the supreme God. ‘The Spirit of Christ’ in the prophets echoes 1 Peter 1:11 (τὸ ἐν αὐτοῖς πνεῦμα Χριστοῦ), a clear allusion, so cited. The Psalm (LXX 148:4–5) has the same number in English; LXX reads αἰνεῖτε αὐτόν, Origen has τὸν θεόν. ἐν τοῖς ὑπεραναβεβηκόσι τὰ αἰσθητά could be neuter (realities beyond sense) or masculine (those who have risen beyond sense); read as neuter to fit ‘the place above the heavens’, rendered ‘what lies beyond the things of sense’. ἀπογινώσκω here = ‘I do not rule out’. Phaedrus 247c, both quotations; Plato has περὶ ἥν, the TEI prints περὶ ὅν (likely a typo or variant), translated by the sense either way. ‘Those very words’ (ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνων τῶν λόγων) = the prophetic words just named, not Plato’s. καθ᾿ ὑπερβολὴν εἰς ὑπερβολήν rendered ‘beyond all measure’.

βαθύτητα τοῦ πλήθους τῶν ... θεωρημάτων: 'the depth and abundance of the truths' changed to 'the depth of the many insights' (genitive kept, not split into two nouns; θεωρήματα = insights, not 'truths'); 'what lies beyond' changed to 'the realms beyond'

Phaedrus sentence corrected: Origen joins the two possibilities ('learned from certain Hebrews and, as some have recorded, had even come upon the prophetic writings'), not 'or'; ἐν οἷς ἔλεγεν rendered 'There he said'
'those very words' made 'those very prophetic words' so the reader does not take ἐκείνων γε τῶν λόγων as Plato's
checked: 1 Peter 1:11, Psalm 148:4–5 (same number in LXX), Phaedrus 247c for both quotations, Second Letter phrase, 2 Corinthians 4:17–18
